kf: **Perioral dermatitis** is a facial eruption of tiny papules and pustules around the mouth, nose or eyes with **sparing next to the lips**.
Commonest in women aged 20–45 and children; often provoked by **topical, inhaled or nasal steroids** and heavy creams.
No comedones (unlike acne); no flushing (unlike rosacea).
Stop steroids and cosmetics, expect a rebound; topical metronidazole or azelaic acid; oral tetracycline for 6–8 weeks if needed.
Children under 12: erythromycin rather than tetracycline.

sub: Women 20–45 most; prepubertal children (often periocular, steroid-related).

aet: Steroids disrupt the barrier and the follicle; occlusive cosmetics; possibly fluorinated toothpaste and microbiome changes.
myths: **"Hydrocortisone will settle it"**: it masks it briefly and then makes it worse.
patho_lead: Steroids and occlusion damage the **barrier around facial follicles**, triggering inflammation.

mech.t: Steroids and heavy creams thin the barrier and alter the follicular microbiome.
Innate immune activation causes small papules and pustules around follicles.
Steroids suppress the rash; stopping causes rebound, so patients reapply.
mech.cap: Perioral dermatitis: papules around the mouth and nose, with a clear rim next to the lips.

mech.t: Stopping the trigger and anti-inflammatory treatment restores the barrier over weeks.

histo: Rarely needed: perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate; granulomatous in the granulomatous variant.

sub: Yellow-brown papules in children of African descent; slower to clear; refer if persistent.

prog: Clears over 6–12 weeks with treatment; recurs if steroids are restarted.
